text: A text from "DHL" says your parcel is stuck in customs — tap the link and pay a €2.99 fee or it gets sent back. What do you do?

answers.text: Pay through the link right away — €2.99 is barely worth worrying about
Ignore the link and, if I'm actually expecting a parcel, check directly in the real DHL app or website using the tracking number
Reply to the text and ask for details
Open the link just to look — I'll only pay if the page looks legit

explanation: Reputable couriers don't demand customs fees via SMS links — treat such links as a scam attempt ("smishing," after your card details). Always check shipments only through the official app/website using the tracking number, never via the link in the message.

text: Which feature most reliably exposes a phishing email pretending to be from your "bank"?

answers.text: The email contains the bank's logo
The email is written in flawless language
The link in the email starts with "https://"
The email tells you to "confirm" your login details via a link immediately, or your account will be locked

explanation: Banks never ask you to "confirm" a password or PIN via an email link and don't threaten instant lockout. A logo, flawless wording, and an "https" prove nothing — every scam page has those too. When in doubt, use the bank app or the address you typed yourself, never the email link.

text: An online shop offers the sought-after game console 70% cheaper than anywhere else. What's the strongest sign of a fake shop?

answers.text: Prepayment/bank transfer only, no seller address or contact details, and the reviews feel generic
The site shows a padlock symbol (https) in the address bar
The shop accepts PayPal buyer protection and credit cards
The product photos look professional

explanation: An unrealistic price + prepayment only + no verifiable seller (company name, address, contact) + generic reviews are the classic fake-shop tells. An https padlock only means the transfer is encrypted, NOT that the shop is legitimate — scammers have SSL too. Payment methods with buyer protection protect you.

text: You land on a login page at the address `paypa1-security.com`. What's wrong here?

answers.text: Nothing — "security" in the name shows it's secure
The page is real as long as it shows the PayPal logo
The domain is fake: `paypa1-security.com` is a separate, unrelated domain, not paypal.com — with a "1" instead of "l" to look genuine
You simply can't tell from the outside

explanation: Scammers register lookalike domains (typos, add-ons, swapped characters like 1↔l or 0↔o). What matters is always the part right before the ending: in `paypa1-security.com` the domain is `paypa1-security`, not PayPal. Read the address carefully or type it yourself.

text: There's a QR-code sticker on the parking meter: "Pay conveniently online here." Why be careful?

answers.text: QR codes can never be dangerous
Stuck-on QR codes can come from scammers and lead to fake payment pages — a code hides its destination until you scan it
Only QR codes in emails are a problem
As long as a payment field appears after scanning, everything's fine

explanation: "Quishing" uses QR codes because you can't see the address behind them. Scammers stick fake codes over real ones on parking meters, charging stations, or in letters. After scanning, check the address shown — or just use the provider's official app instead of unknown codes.

text: What makes a password strongest against automated cracking attempts?

answers.text: Its length — a long passphrase of several random words beats a short, complicated password
As many special characters as possible, like in P@$$!
Bumping it up by one digit at the end on a regular basis
Containing your name plus birth year so you won't forget it

explanation: Length beats complexity — provided the password isn't predictable: each extra random character multiplies the cracking effort. A passphrase of genuinely random words like "bumblebee-battery-cloud-tango7" is both safer AND easier to remember than "P@$$w0rd". Name+birth-year, quotes, and "+1" patterns, by contrast, are easy to guess.

text: Why is a password manager one of the best security decisions?

answers.text: Because it stores passwords unencrypted for fast access
Because then you don't have to remember any master password at all
Because it lets you safely use the same strong password everywhere
Because it generates and encrypts a long, unique password for every service, so a leak at service A doesn't endanger your other accounts

explanation: The biggest win is uniqueness: a separate, random password per service, so one data leak doesn't spill over to your other accounts. The manager remembers them encrypted — you only need ONE strong master password. "Same one everywhere" stays wrong even with a manager.

text: Four common two-factor (2FA) methods — which is the most phishing-resistant?

answers.text: A code sent by SMS to your phone
A passkey or hardware security key — cryptographically bound to the real website
A one-time code from an authenticator app (TOTP)
Approving a push notification in the app

explanation: All four are 2FA methods, but they differ in strength: SMS codes are interceptable (SIM swapping, phishing relay); authenticator apps (TOTP) and push approvals are better but can still be tricked onto a fake page; passkeys/hardware keys are strongest because they're bound to the real domain and simply won't work on a fake site.

text: An online forum had a data breach. Why can that suddenly endanger your email account too?

answers.text: It can't — a forum breach stays with the forum
Only if the forum had stored your credit card
If you use the same password for the forum and your email, scammers automatically try the leaked credentials across many services (credential stuffing)
Only if you used your real name on the forum

explanation: In "credential stuffing," leaked email/password combos are tried automatically against hundreds of other services. Reused passwords turn one small leak into a chain reaction. That's why you want a separate password per service (see password manager).

text: Your "grandchild" calls, the voice sounds convincingly real, they're in trouble and need money by transfer right now. What do you do?

answers.text: Hang up and call back on the number I already know, or verify the family through another channel, before anything happens
Transfer immediately — the voice was clearly real
Ask a few personal questions on the phone; whoever answers them is genuine
Give the money, but only half

explanation: AI can clone a voice from a few seconds of audio — "sounds real" is no longer proof. The protection is always a callback through an independent, known channel. Personal questions help little because much is findable online. Pressure + immediate transfer = alarm signal.

text: On a dating or investment platform, an unusually polished profile messages you, quickly builds trust, then advises a "can't-lose" investment. What's most suspicious?

answers.text: … that the profile picture looks good
… that the person is never willing to do a spontaneous video call, builds emotional closeness fast, and steers toward an investment
… that the person is online in the evenings
… nothing, as long as you haven't sent money yet

explanation: Romance and investment scams use AI-generated photos and chat text. Typical signs: fast "love/trust bombing," excuses to avoid live video calls, and sooner or later a money request. Refusing video calls is a warning sign — but a video call is NOT proof of authenticity (live deepfakes exist). The only safe move: verify identity independently and never send money.

text: In a video, a well-known entrepreneur recommends a crypto platform with "guaranteed doubling." How do you read this?

answers.text: The video is proof — if the person says it, it's true
Legit, because the ad links from a verified-looking account
Legit, because the platform shows small early payouts
Very likely a deepfake or a hijacked ad account — a "guaranteed doubling" is fraudulent, and celebrities are "cloned" for fake ads

explanation: Deepfake videos put fabricated statements into real people's mouths; celebrity "investment tips" are a mass phenomenon. Neither a verified-looking account nor early mini-payouts prove legitimacy. The warning sign is in the promise: legitimate investments never offer a "guaranteed" doubling.

text: It used to be: bad spelling exposes phishing. Why doesn't that rule hold today?

answers.text: Because scammers now employ proofreaders
Because spelling was never a clue
Because AI text tools produce flawless, convincing, personalized messages in any language — watch the content and context, not the typos
Because modern email programs auto-correct typos

explanation: AI has made the "typo" tell worthless: phishing today is linguistically perfect and often personalized. Rely on context — an unexpected request, urgency, a link/attachment, an unusual ask — instead of the language.

text: An email from your "boss" urgently asks you to buy gift cards and send the codes. What's the right response?

answers.text: Verify the request through a second, known channel (call/in person) — real managers don't request this by email
Get it done quickly — the boss is in a hurry
Reply to the email and ask for confirmation
Buy the cards, but only send the codes once the boss gets in touch again

explanation: The "CEO fraud"/gift-card trick runs on authority plus urgency. The countermeasure is always verification through an independent channel — a reply to the email lands with the scammer. Gift-card codes as "payment" are virtually always a scam.

text: An app promises "guaranteed 2% returns — daily." What does your gut tell you (correctly)?

answers.text: Sounds great — I'll invest my savings
Guaranteed 2% daily is not a legitimate investment promise — it's typical Ponzi-scheme bait
Legit, as long as I get small payouts at the start
Legit, as long as friends are joining in too

explanation: Guaranteed + high + regular is the trademark of Ponzi schemes: early mini-payouts are bait, funded by new victims' money; "friends are joining in" is exactly the recruitment mechanism. Legitimate investments fluctuate and guarantee nothing.

text: Which feature is a very common warning sign across many scams?

answers.text: A polite salutation
A long, factual explanation
An offer to think it over at your leisure
Artificial time pressure — "act now, or account locked / fine / opportunity gone"

explanation: Urgency switches off critical thinking — which is why it's a common thread across many scams (phishing, grandparent scam, fake authority, investment fraud). Not every scam uses time pressure (some rely on trust or run unnoticed), but when pressured: pause, do nothing immediately, verify independently. Legitimate parties give you time.

text: A simple flashlight app wants access to your contacts, location, and microphone. What's the right conclusion?

answers.text: These permissions have nothing to do with the function — data is probably being collected and sold; avoid such apps or deny the permissions
Just allow it, otherwise the app might not work
That's normal for every app and harmless
Only apps from small providers collect data

explanation: Permissions should match the function — a flashlight needs neither contacts nor location nor microphone. Excessive permissions point to data collection for ad/data brokers. On your phone, grant permissions individually and deny the unnecessary ones; when in doubt, avoid the app.

text: You're on open airport Wi-Fi and want to quickly do some online banking. What applies?

answers.text: Open Wi-Fi is always completely safe
As long as I'm quick, nothing can happen
Do sensitive things like banking over mobile data or a trustworthy VPN; don't rely on the open network alone
A VPN makes online banking inherently less secure

explanation: On open networks you can never be sure who's listening or whether the hotspot is genuine (fake "Airport_WiFi"). HTTPS protects the content, but for sensitive tasks mobile data is the simplest safe choice. A VPN helps — but only a trustworthy provider; a shady VPN just moves the trust and can become a risk itself.
